title: Your service

lines: YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.
cards: Son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says Allah will speak words like these on the Day of Resurrection.

The person is bewildered: how could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds? And the answer comes: My servant so-and-so was sick, and you did not visit him. Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.
The same exchange follows about food and about water. A hospital room, a hungry stranger, a thirsty one. Khidmah.

teach.b: Khidmah is service, the work of looking after someone else's needs. In Muslim communities you'll hear it for everything from serving tea at a gathering to running a food pantry. Why does service count as worship?
That hadith does something bold. It doesn't put service next to worship. It puts Allah inside the visit.

teach.h: ALLAH FOUND IN THE SICK ROOM.
teach.b: Nobody in the story is praying, and yet the sick room is where Allah is found. How is it meant to be done?

In surah al-Insan, the Qur'an describes people who give food, for love of Him, to the needy, the orphan and the prisoner, and who say: we feed you only for the sake of Allah; we want no reward from you and no thanks.
That's a high bar, and an honest one. Service that waits for applause starts to become about the server. The same hour at a shelter can be a chore, a line on an application, or worship.
The givers in al-Insan say theirs out loud: for the sake of Allah. What changes is what the hour is for.
And the promise. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says Allah is in the help of His servant as long as the servant is in the help of his brother. So service isn't only something given away.
In the tradition's telling, the one who serves is also being served.

how: Muslims serve others through food pantries, hospital visits, mosque kitchens and community volunteering, describing it as khidmah, service, and as worship when done for Allah's sake; a hadith says that whoever visits the sick will find Allah there.

o: paid work done for the mosque by its staff and imam
service to people, given for Allah's sake, without wanting thanks
volunteer hours done to fill a line on a job application

p: you would have found Me with him
no reward from you, no thanks

s: service only counts as worship inside a mosque
in the hadith, Allah says that had you visited the sick person, you would have found Him with him (Sahih Muslim).
the Qur'an describes givers who want no reward and no thanks
surah al-Insan: we feed you only for the sake of Allah; we want no reward from you and no thanks.
the one who serves gives and gets nothing back
Sahih Muslim: Allah is in the help of His servant as long as the servant is in the help of his brother.

games.q: on the Day of Resurrection, a voice says: I was sick and you did not visit Me. you answer: how could I visit You? what comes next?
o: my servant was sick; had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.
you should have prayed more instead.
games.why: in the hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim, Allah points to the sick servant and says, you would have found Me with him. the same follows for food and water.

practice: Let your breath go out a little longer than it comes in, and bring to mind someone who is sick, or alone, or short of something this week, someone real if you can, without trying to fix anything yet.
Let the hadith's question land: if you visited, what would you find there? If you pray, make your intention for Allah; if you don't, simply set your intention to show up without needing thanks.

wordCard.voice: Khidmah. Service to people, given for Allah's sake, without waiting for reward or thanks. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: service, looking after someone's needs.

carryVoice: Your line: serve. No applause needed, because the hour was never about the server. Until tomorrow.
